title: Adjust a rear drum brake: lever the star wheel through the backing-plate slot with a spoon until the drum drags lightly
instruction: Adjust the rear brake so the drum turns with a light drag, then put the spoon down and let go of everything.
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics hold about 0.8 million jobs in the US (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook), and brake work is one of their most common jobs. After new shoes are fitted to a rear drum brake, the self-adjuster is run in, so the shoes sit well inside the drum and the pedal travels too far. The technician puts a brake spoon through the slot in the backing plate onto the adjuster's star wheel and levers it round a click or two at a time, turning the drum with the other hand to feel for the shoes starting to drag, and stops when the drum still turns by hand with a light drag. One click too many and the shoes lock the drum, and the self-adjuster's lever stops the wheel being turned back without pulling it aside. The star wheel is out of sight behind the plate: the blade must find the teeth through the slot and pivot on the slot's edge.
setup: Positions in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A cropped rear drum-brake corner of a car is bolted by its axle stub (70 mm steel tube) to a bench stand (an upright 50 mm square steel post at x = 0.53, y = -0.095, an arm forward to the stub, on a 12 x 12 cm foot plate), its axle along y at x = 0.30, 18 cm above the table. Backing plate: pressed steel, 270 mm across, 3 mm thick, its outboard face at y = -0.05 facing the robot's left, with a 5 mm dust lip; 85 mm below the axle, its adjusting slot is open (22 mm wide, 16 mm tall, rubber plug out). Inside: two new 228 x 50 mm shoes (5 mm linings) spread at the bottom by a self-adjuster: an adjusting screw with a brass star wheel (30 mm across, 10 teeth, 6 mm thick) 42 mm outboard of the plate, its axis along x, 85 mm below the axle, right behind the slot. A spring-loaded lever rides on the teeth: one tooth per click, about 0.10 N m to turn, and it can't turn back. Each click spreads the shoes 0.05 mm toward the drum; they start 1.5 mm inside it. Drum: a cast-iron 9 in (228.6 mm bore, 256 mm outside) rear brake drum, 6 kg, 73 mm deep, on the hub (it turns freely, 0.15 N m of bearing drag), with five M12 wheel studs on a 114.3 mm circle standing 45 mm proud of its face, one at the top. Brake adjusting spoon: 22.5 cm overall: a red moulded plastic handle (100 x 24 x 18 mm) and a flat spring-steel blade (125 x 12 x 1.6 mm), 90 g, lying flat on the table along y, blade toward the corner, handle centre at (0.20, -0.265), blade end at y = -0.09. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Watched every control step (20 Hz); the adjuster's position is counted in clicks of the star wheel (each 0.05 mm of shoe-to-drum clearance, from 1.5 mm at 0 clicks), in the corner's frame. 0 if at any time the shoes are driven onto the drum (30 clicks or more: clearance 0, the drum locked), or the spoon leaves the table (its centre more than 5 cm below the table top). Otherwise, at the end: 0 for no click; 0.5 x clicks / 22 for 1 to 21 clicks (clearance above 0.40 mm: the drum spins freely, with 0.15 to 0.23 N m of drag); 0.75 for 22 to 28 clicks (clearance 0.40 to 0.10 mm: a light drag, 0.31 to 0.8 N m to turn the drum by hand) when the success conditions below are not all met for 1 s; 0.25 for 29 clicks (0.05 mm: a dragging brake, over 4 N m). 1.0 (success, held for 1 s): 22 to 28 clicks, the spoon lying on the table (every part of it within 3 cm of the table top), every part of both grippers at least 2 cm from the spoon and from the drum and its studs, the spoon still (under 1 cm/s) and the drum still (under 4 deg/s). Doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0.
reset_notes: Back the star wheel off to its start (hold the self-adjuster's lever away from the wheel with a thin screwdriver and turn it back to 1.5 mm clearance, checked with a brake shoe gauge), put the spoon back at its mark and turn the drum so a stud is at the top. On a real corner, the clearance is read with a drum-and-shoe gauge (drum bore minus shoe diameter, halved) and the drag with a dial torque wrench on the hub nut.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz. Slot, star wheel teeth, spoon and studs are full-size colliders. The shoes are fixed (their 0.05 mm per click is invisible): clearance comes from counted clicks, and the drum's drag is a joint damping set from it, sized to the torque at 30 deg/s and locked at zero clearance. Detent: a capped spring to the nearest notch; the pawl: a stop 0.6 tooth back. Shoe-to-drum friction is not simulated; drag figures are estimates.
